RIDGEWOOD, N.J. — Today, September 4, 2026, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5), Co-Chair of the House Commission on Artificial Intelligence and the Innovation Economy, unveiled a comprehensive, bipartisan back-to-school agenda to make sure students in the Fifth District and across the country are prepared for a world increasingly shaped by AI. Speaking at George Washington Middle School, Gottheimer announced his new bipartisan AI LABS Act, co-led by Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23), to help K-12 schools build dedicated AI labs and train teachers — and paired it with a broader push to keep phones out of the classroom, protect New Jersey’s phone-free schools resources, boost AI literacy in the classroom, and close the digital divide so no community gets left offline.

Watch full remarks here.

“We’re not going to pretend AI doesn’t exist, and we’re not going to ban it and hope it goes away. So, here in Jersey, we need to do this differently,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “AI can be a powerful tool, but it can never replace the fundamentals. Give our schools the tools. Give our teachers the training. And give our children a real head start, instead of a false choice between banning technology outright and drowning in it.”

AI is already reshaping how students study, how teachers plan, and how employers hire, but K-12 schools have unequal access to the tools and curricula students need to learn how to use it responsibly. The bipartisan AI LABS Act tackles that gap head-on.

This legislation directs the Department of Education to create a new federal grant program or make resources from existing grant programs available to help K-12 schools establish dedicated AI labs, much like the computer and typing labs that became a fixture in schools a generation ago. Those labs would give students hands-on curricula on how to use and understand AI, help teachers better understand the technology, and incorporate it into their classrooms. The bill also directs the Department to study who receives the resources, how they are used, and to make recommendations on future investment so students and educators stay ahead on AI education.

Alongside the AI LABS Act, Gottheimer announced additional steps in his AI back-to-school agenda:

Protecting New Jersey’s phone-free schools resources. Gottheimer is sending a letter to Governor Mikie Sherrill and New Jersey Commissioner of Education Dr. Lily Laux that emphasizes the importance of the state’s Phone-Free Schools Grant Program. Public school districts across Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex counties — including eleven here in the Fifth District — received grants to go bell-to-bell phone-free this year.

Boosting AI education in New Jersey. Gottheimer is calling on the State to dedicate K-12 resources specifically to responsibly integrate AI literacy, ethics, and practical skills into K-12 public school curriculum while limiting screen time to ensure fundamentals remain a priority in education.

Keeping phones out of the classroom. Gottheimer is supporting the bipartisan UNPLUGGED Act, introduced by Representatives Eugene Vindman (VA-7) and Jen Kiggans (VA-2), which supports state and local policies that keep personal electronic devices out of the classroom during school hours. It also establishes a Department of Education grant program to help schools purchase secure lock boxes and pouches, with commonsense exceptions for students with medical needs, disabilities, and English learners.

Ensuring Connectivity for All Students and Families. Gottheimer is sending a letter to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) urging the agencies to prioritize broadband deployment to rural and underserved school districts, so the benefits of AI are not concentrated in the wealthiest, most connected communities. This letter builds on Gottheimer’s work fighting for broadband funding for New Jersey, including more than $260 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill that he helped write, negotiate, and sign into law.

These actions build on Gottheimer’s consistent support for New Jersey schools, including fighting against the Trump administration’s proposed cuts to over $1 billion in education funding for New Jersey, which were fortunately blocked.

Ridgewood Public School District, one of the largest and top-ranked school districts in Bergen County, is implementing a “Return to a Strong Foundation” emphasis this year focused on limiting screens in the classroom and keeping fundamentals front and center in the age of AI.

Gottheimer was joined by Ridgewood Councilman Frank Mortimer, Ridgewood School District Superintendent Dr. Mark Schwarz, George Washington Middle School Principal Dave Bailey, Bergen County Association of School Administrators President Dr. Joseph Cirillo, NJ PTA President Jackie Gibbs, NJ PTA Federal Legislative Chairperson Sharon Roseboro, and NJ PTA Bergen County Council of PTAs President Nancy Wallace. Gottheimer was also joined by four George Washington Middle School students involved in student government – Alaiya Barnes, Landon Ponchak, Karleigh Cadaret, and Druv Kethini.

Below: Gottheimer announces Bipartisan Back-to-School Agenda on AI and Screen Time in K-12 Education.

Read full remarks here:

Good morning, Ridgewood!

As you close out your first week back to school, I want to start by thanking everyone here at George Washington Middle School, including the educators, the administrators and staff, the school board, and especially the students, for having me here today.

Now, I did a little homework before I came, because that’s what you’re supposed to do at school, right? And, I learned a couple of things about this building that I did not know.

First, some of you know the name Willie Geist. He anchors Sunday Today and co-hosts Morning Joe. Willie met his wife, Christina, in their sixth-grade homeroom right here at George Washington Middle School, back in 1986. Forty years later, they’re still together. So, I don’t know exactly what they were teaching in that homeroom, but whatever it was, keep doing it.

Second, Ridgewood’s roots go all the way to the Revolutionary War. George Washington visited this area and wrote letters from right around here, while Patriot and British troops fought nearby. The borough was practically founded during America’s fight for independence. When Washington delivered his first Annual Address to Congress, he said something I think about a lot, especially on a day like today. He said, “Knowledge is in every country the surest basis of public happiness.”

Two hundred and fifty years after our founding, that’s still true, and it’s exactly why we’re here this morning.

I want to give real credit to the Ridgewood School District. While you study the past, you’re not living it. You’re on the cutting edge of education, including how to best use, and not use, technology to learn. This year, you launched your “Return to a Strong Foundation” initiative, cutting back laptop use in the classroom for its nearly 5,500 students, especially for the youngest children. Ridgewood started limiting cell phones in school, too, with phones in lockers, all day, for every student, from elementary school right up through high school. I should add that’s now the state law. No phones in the classroom.

In my opinion, that’s exactly the kind of commonsense, community-driven leadership we need more of, and it’s exactly the balance we need to be talking about in the age of AI. The answer isn’t more screens. The answer is smarter, more purposeful use of technology, alongside real, honest-to-goodness reading, writing, and critical thinking. In other words, technology can’t do your work or your thinking for you. When the calculator showed up to replace the abacus, we still learned how to count. As a kid, I used to look up facts in the World Book Encyclopedia – and then came the Internet.

I still got to read about and learn about the landing on the moon, but I found the information online, not in a book on the shelf. There’s a big difference. We can’t let AI write our papers or do our math assignments, but it can be a tool for helping us learn. We can’t allow AI to replace our educators, but it can certainly help take the busy work off their plate, or allow them to develop more personalized lesson plans for students.

It’s clear that your school system and your educators already get that. Today, I’m here to take that approach across our state and nationwide.

We are at a true inflection point. Technology isn’t slowing down for us. It never has and never will. Just this week, OpenAI introduced Astra, its latest model. This is on the heels of Anthropic’s Mythos – and new Chinese open-weight models that are coming at us nearly every week.

Whether we like it or not, artificial intelligence, or AI, is already in our children’s backpacks, on their laptops, and on their phones. The question isn’t whether our children will encounter AI in their lives – K-12, in college, in their jobs. They will. Just the way we have iPhones and our parents didn’t.

The question is whether we prepare them for it, or just cross our fingers and hope for the best.

Obviously, we can’t take that chance. Our children absolutely need every tool available to compete, not just against others in New Jersey or in the US, but against children in China, India, and all over the world already being trained on this technology. If we sit on our hands, if we don’t have the tools, we will fall behind. That’s just the reality.

But, I want to be really clear about this. AI can be a powerful tool, but it can never replace the fundamentals.

Our students need to learn how to think, solve problems, ask questions, and understand the material for themselves, not through a chatbot. We should use AI to strengthen those skills – not use it as a shortcut around them.

Here’s why I say that. A recent poll found that 45 percent of Jersey students report using AI frequently for schoolwork. But, here’s the number that should get every parent’s attention: nearly two out of three students admit they’ve used AI to cheat in school. And nationally, the majority of teens think AI cheating happens regularly at their own school.

Meanwhile, a lot of parents are flying blind – and, while there are some tools to help, it’s not always easy for an educator to catch a kid using AI to do his or her assignment. In a recent survey from Montclair School District, half of parents said they had no idea how often their own kid uses AI for schoolwork, and 87 percent said they want clearer communication from schools about all of it. So, we’ve got children using a powerful new technology every single day, and we’ve got parents and teachers who, in far too many cases, don’t even know it’s happening, let alone whether it’s helping or hurting their student or child.

Now, some places have looked at all this and panicked. This week, Mayor Mamdani and New York City rolled out a policy banning AI tools outright for every student through eighth grade, with only high schoolers getting restricted access.

I get the instinct. Fewer screens, more critical thinking. I agree with that part, one hundred percent – and I think a lot more of our tests and note-taking should be on a piece of paper, not a computer. But, an outright ban doesn’t teach a single kid how to use AI responsibly, nor does it teach the skills that can help them.

It just guarantees that the first time they really encounter AI with no guardrails and no guidance is the day they get handed a diploma and shoved into a workforce that runs on this stuff. That’s not a plan. That’s sticking your head in the sand and hoping it goes away.

Think about it this way. When I was a kid, we had typing class. Some of you probably did too, pecking away on those big clunky keyboards.

Then by the 80s, and into the ’90s, schools built computer labs because people realized that if children don’t learn a new technology in school that would prepare them for life, in a structured way, with a teacher guiding them, they will learn it somewhere else: badly, unsupervised, and usually too late.

AI technology is the same idea for this generation. We’re not going to pretend it doesn’t exist, and we’re not going to ban it and hope it goes away. So, here in Jersey, we need to do this differently.

We should put AI skills in a classroom, with a curriculum, with an educator, and with guardrails, so that our children grow up to be smart users of AI, not passive victims of it.

That’s why, today, I’m announcing my new bipartisan AI LABS Act, with my colleague Congressman Jay Obernolte of California. This federal legislation directs the U.S. Department of Education to create a new federal grant program to help K-12 public schools set up dedicated AI labs, with real curricula, that teach students how AI actually works, and how to be prepared to utilize it smartly in the new AI world.

This builds on recommendations from the American Federation of Teachers and the National Education Association for real, dedicated curricula that are directed and supervised by educators. There is a reason why AI companies are now hiring college students with philosophy and history degrees, not just those with computer science degrees. They want people who can think critically. The trades also want young people who know how to use AI on the shop floor and in building and manufacturing.

That means learning how to use AI, how to question it, and how to know when to – and not to — trust it. My new legislation will also help teachers get trained up, too, so they’re not scrambling to keep pace with their own students. It also requires a study on how the funds are actually being utilized, so we know what’s working and can keep improving it.

I don’t want to raise a generation of children who can prompt a chatbot, but can’t write a paragraph on their own, or think through what question to ask the chatbot.

I want to raise a generation of children who can use it to genuinely improve their work, because they understand how to use it and know its limits.

That’s the whole idea behind the AI LABS Act. Give our schools the tools. Give our teachers the training. And give our children a real head start, instead of a false choice between banning technology outright and drowning in it.

Second, I’m sending a letter to Governor Sherrill and Education Commissioner Laux on the State’s Phone-Free Schools Grant Program. That program has already helped eighty-six school districts, including eleven right here in the Fifth District. It puts real bell-to-bell cell phone policies in place, with secure pouches, lockers, and the staff training to make it actually work.

Here’s the problem: The current budget for next year includes a record $12.4 billion for K-12 education, but there’s no dedicated earmark in there to keep this program going in the future.

My letter emphasizes the importance of this funding – school districts are just starting to get this right, and we can’t pull the rug out from under them now.

Third, I’m also pushing for new federal funding to help supplement the state’s program. That’s why, I’m very proud to cosponsor the bipartisan UNPLUGGED Act – legislation that directs states and school districts to actually implement phone-free policies during the school day, and it creates a federal grant program to help schools pay for the lockboxes and secure pouches to make it happen.

It includes sensible exceptions too, for children managing a medical condition like Type 1 diabetes, children with disabilities, and English language learners who need translation support.

More resources for this important effort will help implement New Jersey’s new cell phone ban legislation that previous Governor Murphy signed into law in January, which requires all school districts in the state to adopt policies restricting the use of cell phones and other internet-enabled devices in K-12 public schools.

Fourth, I’m working with the state to keep building out real K-12 AI literacy priorities. This builds on New Jersey’s Department of Education’s new core AI principles that were developed with TeachAI, a global partnership that helps schools and governments use AI safely and responsibly in education. These principles will ensure Jersey schools keep people in the loop and put students’ own thinking front and center, not just whatever the AI spits out. This is exactly the kind of approach we need.

We can’t risk losing funding for this program. That’s why, along with others, I successfully fought the Trump Administration’s proposed cuts to New Jersey’s schools. He tried to gut more than $1 billion in federal funding – and we beat him.

And finally, I’m writing to the FCC and the NTIA about broadband access and connectivity. This is an issue that I’ve been working on for years, and, while we’ve made a ton of progress, we still have towns in Northern Jersey with basically dial-up connectivity, and speeds that AI can’t run on. That’s unacceptable.

Right now, there are more than 5,000 homes in Sussex County without dial up, with more than 3,000 more who don’t have access to broadband.

If we don’t get high-speed internet into our rural and disadvantaged school districts, like parts of Sussex County that I represent — net inequality will be permanently baked in. The advantages that AI promises shouldn’t depend on your zip code. I am urging both agencies to prioritize the communities furthest behind, so they get connected first, not last.

This builds on my work getting hundreds of millions in funding for broadband infrastructure right here in Jersey through the American Rescue Plan, the Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill, and the CARES Act, three historic bills that I helped write, negotiate, and sign into law. I’m calling on the state to put to work the money that I fought for in the Care Act. New Jersey was approved for more than $260 million that I helped bring back from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. So far, only $60 million has been deployed to help connect Jersey families, but we have a long way to go.

Right now, the Trump administration is holding up the last $200 million of this critical funding to connect families across Sussex County and the rest of the state. That’s why the FCC and the administration need to release the rest of the funds and get broadband access to every family across the state.

Put it all together, and here’s what we’re doing today: a bill to teach AI the right way, and a push to keep phones out of the way, a push to get real funding for AI literacy, and a push to make sure no community in America gets left offline while the rest of the world races ahead.

I’ll be honest with you: as Co-chair of the House Commission on AI, technology is moving fast, and some days it can feel like it’s moving faster than we can keep up with. But, I have never once bet against American children and Jersey’s incredible educators and schools – and I’m not about to start today.

I promise you, these children will run circles around whatever the future throws at them.

As long as we keep investing in our children and working together, here in the greatest country in the world, I know that our best days will always, always be ahead of us.

Thank you, God bless you, and may God continue to bless and watch over the United States of America.

WASHINGTON, DC —Today, Representative Josh Riley (NY-19) and Representative Mike Kennedy (UT-03) introduced the Smart Meter Data Privacy Protection Act, bipartisan legislation to ban utility companies from selling Upstate New Yorkers’ private data and crack down on the misuse of personal information collected through smart meters.

Upstate New York’s utility monopolies rolled out smart meters under the guise of streamlining billing, and hit customers who declined to install one with extra fees. Customers who keep their analog meters pay NYSEG a monthly opt-out fee of $13.47 per month, while Central Hudson charges a one time fee of $49 for electric meters and $89 for gas meters.

But the meters do far more than track energy use: they capture detailed, real-time information on household energy patterns, daily routines and habits — data that industry analysts call a “holy grail” for marketers and data aggregators. The sale of smart-meter data is projected to grow into a billion-dollar industry.

The Smart Meter Data Privacy Protection Act mandates that utilities can only use customers’ energy-usage data for core functions like billing, grid reliability, outages, and regulatory compliance. The legislation also prevents utility companies from selling or sharing customer data without consent.

“Nobody asked for smart meters. The utilities rolled them out anyway, and if you didn’t want one, they charged you extra just to opt out,” said Riley. “Now they’re raking in millions selling all the data the smart meters collect — when you turn the lights on, when you cook dinner, when you take a shower, even when you shut the TV off at night. Upstate New Yorkers are already paying the foreign-owned utility monopolies too damn much. They shouldn’t get to cash in on our private information, too.”

The bill also requires utilities to give customers monthly reports explaining what data was collected, how it was used, and who it was shared with. Under Riley’s legislation, if a utility improperly profits from a customer’s data, it must pay that customer back through bills credits equal to the revenue it earned from the misuse.

“We must be certain to protect Americans’ personal privacy. Smart meters can reveal families’ daily routines in granular detail, but no one should have to surrender their personal data just to keep the lights on,” said Kennedy. “I am proud to join Rep. Josh Riley in this effort to protect Americans’ right to privacy and make clear that their personal data should not be a commodity.”

This bill builds on Riley’s work to stand up to the utility monopolies on behalf of Upstate New Yorkers:

Condemning ICE’s Abuse of Power & Harmful Tactics in Connecticut

[Hartford, CT] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, held a public forum to receive testimony from the Danbury community about Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)’s destructive and indiscriminate detentions last week. Prior to the forum, Blumenthal and Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves walked through downtown Danbury meeting with city residents and businessowners whose family members were detained by ICE. Blumenthal also joined a rally Wednesday evening to stand in solidarity with the Danbury community as they grapple with the escalating ICE activity in their community.

“The stories I heard in Danbury about ICE’s abuses were gripping & heartbreaking. I will be fighting to hold ICE accountable & ensure justice for detainees & their families,” wrote Blumenthal with an accompanying video on Twitter/X.

As Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Blumenthal has led an investigation into DHS’s abuses. Blumenthal’s forum in Danbury on Thursday follows four public forums hosted by Blumenthal and U.S. Representative Robert Garcia (D-CA), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, as part of their ongoing inquiry into the lawless and abusive tactics used by federal immigration agents:

In March, Blumenthal and Garcia hosted a forum to receive public testimony from young people, mothers, and a school administrator about DHS’s reckless disregard for the safety of children. Prior to the forum, Blumenthal and Garcia released a report entitled “Cruelty is the Point: How Trump’s Immigration Agenda Endangers Children,” which documented 128 children who have been injured left unattended or otherwise put at direct risk of harm as a result of operations by DHS personnel.

In February, Blumenthal and Garica hosted a public forum on constitutional violations and abuses by ICE. The forum featured testimony from Ryan Schwank, a whistleblower who spoke publicly for the first time about his experience as an Instructor for the incoming “surge” of new ICE recruits at the ICE Academy at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center (“FLETC”) in Glynco, Georgia. Teyana Gibson Brown, a U.S. citizen and resident of Minneapolis, Minnesota, also testified about ICE agents forcefully entering her home without a judicial warrant, breaking down her door and pointing guns at her family. Stevan Bunnell, the General Counsel for the Department of Homeland Security from 2013 to 2017, testified as well.

Also in February, Blumenthal and Garcia hosted a forum to receive testimony on the violent tactics and disproportionate use of force by DHS agents. The forum featured testimony from Brent and Luke Ganger, brothers of Renee Nicole Macklin Good, and Antonio Romanucci, the attorney representing their family; Marimar Martinez, Aliya Rahman, and Martin Daniel Rascon, all of whom were violently assaulted by DHS agents; and Seth Stoughton, a former police officer and Professor at the University of South Carolina School of Law.

In December, Blumenthal and Garcia received testimony from five U.S. citizens who were assaulted, detained, and denied their constitutional rights by DHS agents. The forum featured testimony from Americans across the country: Wilmer Chavarria, from Vermont; Dayanne Figueroa, from Illinois; Javier Ramirez, from California; George Retes, from California; and Andrea Velez, from California.

Blumenthal also wrote Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and the Acting Director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) David Venturella requesting a meeting and demanding information about a dramatic increase in immigration enforcement activity in Connecticut over the last several weeks. The surge has focused on Danbury and nearby towns, where people have been targeted dropping their children off at school and going to work.

“Over the past week, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”) agents have sown fear and panic among parents, children, and workers as they detained scores of people in Danbury and other towns in Connecticut. What should have been a time of excitement and community as children in Connecticut return to school has quickly turned into a time of genuine terror,” Blumenthal wrote.

“ICE’s actions in Connecticut showcased cruelty and brutality, as well as disregard for the safety and well-being of community members, especially children. They fostered an environment of fear that will undoubtedly impact school attendance rates and the emotional health of students, generally.”

The full text of Blumenthal’s letter is available here.

On Twitter/X, Blumenthal further slammed the harmful tactics used by ICE agents in Danbury and in communities across the country.

“Cruelty is the point. ICE’s goal is to sow fear in communities like Danbury. While we push for reforms in Congress, we’ll support efforts to fight for justice owed to people detained,” wrote Blumenthal with an accompanying video on Twitter/X.

Demanding Answers About Trump’s Executive Order Restricting Mail-In Voting

After receiving information from a whistleblower, Blumenthal wrote Postmaster General David Steiner demanding answers and documents about the United States Postal Service’s (USPS) rushed and potentially unlawful implementation of President Trump’s Executive Order seeking to restrict mail-in voting.

“This brave whistleblower has come forward with disturbing details about USPS’ seemingly illegal plot to interfere in November’s midterms,” Blumenthal said. “Their system is set up to fail – and risk the right to vote for millions of Americans who cast their ballots by mail. Given this new information, such sloppiness and haste seems clearly part of a purposeful attempt to create chaos and prevent people from voting. I am demanding answers and accountability.”

“The crown jewel of American democracy—our historic record of free and fair elections—deserves better than this reckless, slapdash effort,” said David Kligerman, Senior Vice President and Special Counsel at WhistleblowerAid.org, which represents the anonymous whistleblower. “Given this administration’s record on curtailing voting rights, these glaring issues in the ballot mail program raise a troubling question: are these bugs—or features? Now that these malignant flaws have been exposed by a brave whistleblower, the administration can choose to fix this dangerously haphazard program or barrel ahead toward a wholly preventable electoral disaster.”

An anonymous whistleblower disclosure provided to Blumenthal includes new details about USPS’s attempts to build an online system, known as “the Portal,” and accompanying IT which will be used to screen ballots submitted by state election officials prior to USPS agreeing to mail them to voters. According to this whistleblower, USPS began work on the Portal a mere three-and-a-half months before it was meant to be deployed and has not put it through the standard testing an online system and its related IT like this typically requires. USPS has also reportedly implemented an impracticable zero percent failure rate that could result in a massive number of rejected ballots with no opportunity for appeal.

In April, Blumenthal joined U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-CA), Gary Peters (D-MI), and Dick Durbin (D-IL) in introducing the Absentee and Mail Voter Protection Act (Absentee MVP Act), which would block President Trump’s illegal and unconstitutional executive order attacking mail and absentee ballots and protect the right to vote by mail.

Blumenthal’s letter to Postmaster General Steiner, which includes the whistleblower’s disclosure, is available here.

On Twitter/X, Blumenthal reacted to the USPS’s statement on the development of a U.S. Federal Ballot Mail Portal.

“Absolutely nothing in the Postal Service’s statement denies or contradicts the deeply disturbing details of the whistleblower’s disclosure. Most importantly, it does nothing to directly address the fears of voters that USPS will refuse to deliver their ballots based on the output of a shoddy computer system they started building four months ago. ‘Just trust us’ is not acceptable. The Postal Service stated their commitment to transparency & accountability so I look forward to their detailed response to my specific questions & production of documents,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Slamming FanDuel for Misleading Response to Inquiry About Promo Video Targeting Gambling Addict

Blumenthal and U.S. Representatives Paul Tonko (D-NY) and Valerie Foushee (D-NC) demanded answers after FanDuel refused to adequately respond to the lawmakers’ questions about disturbing reports that the sportsbook repeatedly targeted problem gamblers with predatory perks to keep them trapped in their addiction, including with a personal message from Philadelphia Phillies first baseman, Bryce Harper. Last month, the lawmakers wrote to FanDuel, Major League Baseball (MLB), and the Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA) demanding answers about the policies that enabled this predatory promotion.

In a follow-up letter sent to FanDuel Chief Executive Officer Christian Genetski, the lawmakers called out the sportsbook for providing “misleading and incomplete” responses to their initial inquiry and for failing to adequately address its exploitative VIP services and perks.

“We remain unconvinced that FanDuel is making an active effort to protect bettors from harmful gambling and instead appears to be promoting addiction. We demand real answers to our previous letter and for FanDuel to explain this complete failure to respond to significant matters of public interest,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers continued, “In its August 14th response, FanDuel failed to answer our questions about the specific steps taken to vet and monitor VIP activities, the extent to which VIP managers have encouraged problem gambling with other customers (including such videos), and any changes that it will make to its VIP program after this indefensible conduct.”

The lawmakers continued, “Moreover, in its response, FanDuel fails to demonstrate any commitment to its customers’ well-being through any meaningful limitations on exploitative and dangerous marketing and business practice. FanDuel also boasts of its work with state regulators to meet requirements for licensed sportsbooks and other state laws on gambling yet fails to mention how its prediction markets app, FanDuel Predicts, undermines the integrity of—if not bypasses—those very regulations. FanDuel’s so-called ‘commitment’ to its customers rings especially hollow when it is pushing out harmful and addictive features such as VIP perks, constant push notifications, and personalized promotions.”

Urging Support for Kidnapped Ukrainian Children

Blumenthal and U.S. Senator Thom Tillis (R-NC) along with U.S. Representatives Marcy Kaptur (D-OH) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) wrote Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging him to move quickly in awarding $25 million the State Department has made available to “support the identification, return, rehabilitation, and reintegration of Ukrainian children forcibly transferred to Russia and Russian-occupied territories.”

Although the funding was announced in March, it has not yet been distributed. An estimated 20,000 Ukrainian children have been forcibly transferred to Russia or areas in Ukraine occupied by Russia.

“While we understand the need for rigorous review, thousands of kidnapped Ukrainian children remain separated from their families, and every delay extends the pain and suffering they and their families have already endured,” the members wrote.
